Machaerus
muh-KEER-us
proper noun (a fortress of Herod)
Greek Machairous, from machaira (a sword or dagger); the hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea, the traditional and historical site of John the Baptist's imprisonment and beheading.

Biblical Definition

Machaerus was the fortress-palace of Herod Antipas, perched on a height east of the Dead Sea in Perea, the place where, according to the historian Josephus and the constant tradition of the church, John the Baptist was imprisoned and beheaded. The Gospels do not name the fortress but record the events that took place there. Herod had laid hold on John and bound him in prison for Herodias' sake, his brother Philip's wife, whom he had unlawfully married, because John had told him plainly, “It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife.” Herodias nursed a quarrel and would have killed him, but feared the people and Herod's own reverence for the just and holy man. The occasion came at Herod's birthday feast, when the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him, and he swore to give her whatsoever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she demanded the head of John the Baptist in a charger; and the king, sorry yet bound by his oath and his guests, sent an executioner, who beheaded John in the prison. The dictionary marks Machaerus as the scene of a martyrdom that displays the courage of the faithful prophet who would not flatter a king's sin, the murderous power of a guilty conscience and a vengeful woman, and the folly of the rash oath that snared a weak ruler into innocent blood. John, of whom the Lord said none greater had been born of women, died in a dungeon for the truth, the forerunner sealing in blood the testimony he bore in life.

Webster 1828 Definition

Herod Antipas' hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea, the historical site of John the Baptist's imprisonment and beheading (Mark 6:17-27); the scene of a martyrdom that exposes guilty power, a vengeful queen, and a rash oath.

MACHAERUS, proper noun. [Greek machaira, a sword.] Herod Antipas' fortress east of the Dead Sea.

The historical and traditional site of John the Baptist's imprisonment and death.

Herod bound John for rebuking his unlawful marriage to Herodias (Mark 6:17).

At Herod's birthday feast, Herodias' daughter demanded John's head.

Bound by his rash oath, Herod sent and beheaded John in the prison (Mark 6:27).

Key Scripture

Mr 6:17 — "For Herod himself had sent forth and laid hold upon John, and bound him in prison for Herodias' sake, his brother Philip's wife: for he had married her."

Mr 6:27 — "And immediately the king sent an executioner, and commanded his head to be brought: and he went and beheaded him in the prison,"

Mt 14:3 — "For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias' sake, his brother Philip's wife."

Mt 14:10 — "And he sent, and beheaded John in the prison."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the modern flattery of power that excuses what John condemned, and the loss of the prophet's example of fearless reproof.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prophet's duty to reprove sin even in the seats of power. John the Baptist lost his head because he told a king plainly, “It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife.” The modern instinct, eager to flatter the powerful and to call all private arrangements nobody's business, would have counselled John to silence. The dictionary holds up his example: the faithful witness names sin as sin, whatever the cost, and does not trim the word of God to please a Herod.

Machaerus also exposes the anatomy of a weak and guilty soul. Herod feared John, heard him gladly, and did many things; yet he kept his unlawful wife, bound himself with a drunken oath, feared the opinion of his guests more than the blood of a righteous man, and so was trapped into murder. The dictionary marks the lesson: the man who will not part with his cherished sin will be driven by it to worse, and the fear of man and the rash vow are snares that have destroyed many. John's martyrdom, sealed in that grim fortress, stands as the crown of a life that feared God and not the king.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek machaira (a sword or dagger); the fortress is named by Josephus as the place of John's death, confirmed by the church's tradition.

expand to see more

Machaira, Greek, a sword or large knife, the root of the fortress's name.

A hilltop stronghold of Herod the Great, inherited and used by Herod Antipas.

Located in Perea, east of the Dead Sea, in the territory of Antipas.

Named by the historian Josephus as the site of John the Baptist's death.

The Gospels record the events without naming the fortress (Mark 6; Matthew 14).

Usage

"The pastor preached the death at Machaerus to show that a faithful prophet reproves sin even in a king."

"He warned that Herod's rash oath and fear of his guests trapped him into innocent blood."

"She honoured John, who died in a dungeon for the truth he would not soften."
